p29: 29.  On 6 March 2009, at T.’s request, the Latvian Central Authority asked the “Bāriņtiesa” to enquire into the child’s living conditions and to serve on the applicant T.’s request to see the child.
p30: 30.  On 14 March 2009, during a chance encounter near a shopping centre, T. met the applicant and E. Taking advantage of the situation, he took E., drove her to Tallinn (Estonia) and then began the journey back to Australia. On 16 March 2009 the Latvian Central Authority, at the request of its Estonian counterpart and with a view to allowing T. to board a flight to Helsinki, sent the latter information concerning T.’s right to return to Australia with his daughter.
p31: 31.  Subsequently, a complaint of abduction lodged by the applicant was unsuccessful, as were a disciplinary complaint against the Latvian Central Authority and the request for a stay of execution, which had become devoid of purpose.
p32: 32.  In September 2009 the Australian Family Court revoked all previous decisions concerning the parents’ rights and held that T. had sole parental responsibility for the child. While prohibiting the applicant from discussing in public any matter concerning the child or T., it authorised her to visit her daughter under the supervision of a social worker. The court also prohibited her, firstly, from speaking to her daughter in Latvian and, secondly, until the child reached the age of eleven, from visiting or contacting by any means whatsoever the childcare centres and pre-school or school establishments in which her daughter was enrolled, and the parents of any other child enrolled in those centres and establishments.
p33: 33.  Before the Grand Chamber the Government, referring to an article published in the Latvian press in October 2011 which contained, among other things, statements made by the applicant’s sister, stated that the applicant had gone back to live in Australia, that she had accommodation there and that she was working in a public social-welfare institution. They further stated that she maintained regular contact with her daughter, meeting her twice a week at a social centre, and that she had been able to see her without a social worker being present.
